utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, your honour. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today is Tuesday, the 22nd of May. Good morning to the witness. Good morning to the OTP, to the Defence counsel, and to all the accused, as well to everyone assisting the Trial Chamber. The examination-in-chief will continue. The registrar has informed me that the Prosecution still has one hour and 50 minutes. Mr. Kruger, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President, good morning Your Honours, everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. If we may start by just briefly referring back to something we touched upon yesterday, and that was when General Roso replaced General Praljak in November. Was there any discussion or any views within the international community or the ECMM as to the reason why this had happened? Did you form any opinions?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had general discussions as to whether perhaps Mr. Praljak had not delivered what he was expected to deliver during his period of command. The other stories that we heard were of illness. We were unable to draw any specific conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say that he did not deliver, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday I referred to an expectation that there may be some military activity launched from the area of the Makljen ridge, an offensive action. We didn't witness that offensive action or, if it was, it was no more than regular skirmishing, and perhaps one could surmise that there was an anticipated attack which never materialised and that Mr. Praljak was, as a result of that failure, removed, but that is just my speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can return to where we left off yesterday, and if I can briefly refer you to document or Exhibit 07342. 07342. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is a daily summary by CC Mostar dated 26 December 1993. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a document that I wrote, although it's not signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we can look under Political, paragraph 1, and this is where M1 met Zaim Bakovic in Konjic, and then halfway that paragraph, the discussion is kind of summarised, but halfway down it says, "With regard to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Bakovic acknowledged that there was a part of BiH Herceg-Bosna that was 99 per cent Croat and would never belong to BiH again." Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Bakovic is referring to the area of Herceg-Bosna around Mostar and to the north. That was, by the time this was written, almost exclusively populated by Bosnian Croats, and it seems to me an acknowledgement that he thinks that neither militarily or politically will that be a part of BiH again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The use of "again" at the end, does that signify anything?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it was part of BiH and indeed still is so his conclusion wasn't correct, but what he was saying is there appeared to be a break away, and of course the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was the establishment of a state that signalled a break from the internationally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can look a bit further down under Military, the section for Military, the second paragraph. Yesterday, you mentioned that there were always rumours of presence of HV units or elements in Herceg-Bosna or in the area, and you only saw these units personally in January 1994, but if we look at this paragraph, Fazlic claimed the presence of two HV brigades in the area of Vrdi, but if we can look at your comment specifically. "These allegations are repeated so frequently that they have become fact to many commentators. Only circumstantial evidence of their existence has been -- has ever been presented," and the comment ends. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think probably shows a little bit of frustration on my part. It was something that everybody was interested in, as I referred to yesterday, and it had become a fact, established fact when we as observers on the ground hadn't actually seen it. There-- the repetition continually and the stated claim had become, I think, in international circles an established fact and what I'm saying here is, I've been in the territory for some time. I've heard these. I've looked. I cannot verify them, and until they are, they remain accusations. As far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can turn to a different area now. Could you tell the Court about the economic situation within the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna for the inhabitants, and with specific reference then to Muslim and then Croat inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The picture was very different depending on whether you were a Bosnian Croat or Bosnian Muslim. The economic situation, and by that I mean sort of access to normal, everyday things that we need to live, food and transport and travel, that was as a Bosnian Croat quite possible. You were able to move freely within the area of Herzegovina up to the front line, so that would be up as far as Prozor, and also across the border into Croatia, and there was economic activity between the two states. However, the moment you crossed the front line and went -- went to East Mostar, the situation was completely different. The contrast was stark, and the situation for those living in East Mostar was very bad. There was a dependency on international community for supplies. Not a total dependency. There were supplies coming out of Central Bosnia and down to Mostar and various deals being done, as unlikely as it seems, between the Muslims and the Serb forces, but we had a concentration of civilian population in East Mostar that was short of food and very little electricity supply, if any, and water dependency by the time that I was there was from the Neretva itself, and I saw situations, circumstances there which were worse than anywhere else I observed in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in due course again. If we can step onto the HVO military at this stage. Now, sir, you mentioned earlier that you had testified in the Blaskic case in the appeals case, and not course of your evidence there you expressed that Colonel Blaskic may have had some problems with regard to command and control in Central Bosnia. Could you perhaps just explain to the Court briefly.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in Central Bosnia for the Croats contrasted strongly with that of the Croats in Herzegovina in terms of the military situation and command. You had a commander, General -- or Colonel Blaskic, command of operational zone middle Bosna, who was actually only able to move freely within the pocket that -- which -- that he was in, which was Vitez, and to a lesser extent he could -- he could get down to -- to Kiseljak. So he was commanding troops ostensibly on paper as far as Vares and Zepce and Zavidovici, but he couldn't physically get there and communications were difficult, so he had a fragmented command, control, and communications structure. That would contrast with the structure that would exist within the territory in -- north of Mostar and up to Prozor, where normal lines of communication, command, and control could exist. So commanders from Mostar could visit the front line, whereas Tihomir Blaskic in Central Bosnia wasn't able to go to Zepce, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The HVO military -- the military wing thereof was a relatively young military organisation, as you would be aware at that time when you were there. Could you comment, and this probably falls back on your military training, on how that may have affected the command and control of that force by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly changed during the period that I was there, but when I was in Central Bosnia it was very clear that the HVO -- HVO units, as indeed was the case with the armija, were not equipped in the way one would expect, i.e., there was a mixture of uniform, there was a mixture of weapons, you may have a soldier with a combat top but wearing jeans, and so one had a feeling of a militia rather than an established army. Over time that did change but in Herzegovina you got the impression of a -- of a military structure. There was common uniform, common arms, and so you got -- you had the impression of formed military rather than militia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you comment on the HVO's ability to achieve its objectives in -- with reference to the manpower that it possessed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The received wisdom was that the HVO was better equipped in terms of equipment. In other words, it had access to larger calibre weapons, some artillery and tanks but in terms of manpower the advantage was seen to be with the armija forces. More lightly armed but more soldiers on the front line. The other aspect of the HVO is that we observed that perhaps the ambitions of its military capability in terms of action had not been realised in Central Bosnia. We'd actually seen HVO forces losing territory in Central Bosnia. So there was by the time of, I would say the summer of 1993, most of the front lines had stabilised. There were some specific shifts and alterations, but essentially they had stabilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The -- you say that the HVO had -- had heavier equipment or access to heavier equipment. I'd like to refer you in this regard to Exhibit 03771. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: On its face it's a daily infosum of 28 July 1993, and it's directed to the various regional centres and various teams and various coordination centres, and do you know of this document or can you comment on the origin?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is from Eclo Kiseljak, and Eclo was the EC liaison officer. This was an ECMM officer who sat in the headquarters of the UNPROFOR military headquarters and exchanged information. So he would pass the reports that we were writing to the military structure and likewise would see the military information summaries and give us a briefing, and this is one of his briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to the third page of this document in the Beese version this would be on page 5, and it's paragraph F, titled Prozor, on that page. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, in the middle of that paragraph it reports that at -- and the time code is given on the 27th of July, "Three coaches, 10 to 15 cars, two ambulances were noticed moving on route Triangle. These were clearly identified as HVO [as read] troops and were probably part of the return rotation of HV troops which began on 26 July." And if we then just look at the comment, it says that it's believed that at least two T-55 are on the Podovi feature, and then at the very end of that section it says, "the Rama Brigade is not credited with such assets." Could you comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just looking at the screen and without being pedantic, I think there's one place you've motioned HVO and I think you meant HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the thrust of the question is very clear. The -- this was -- as I had mentioned earlier, would have been witnessed by UNPROFOR rather than ECMM. It is a detailed statement of the equipment, and it includes tanks, the T55. It includes multi-barrel rocket launchers and a statement of three coaches, presumably with -- with troops on board. This is a formed military unit and there's credibility here that this is equipment that belongs to the HV. Whether it's actually being staffed or manned by the HV is different, but it's a very strong indication that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The conclusion, which says "the Rama Brigade is not credited with such assets," can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Rama Brigade in Prozor may well have had access to some heavier weaponry. It might -- they may have had, you know, one tank and a couple of artillery pieces, but here we're seeing on a scale which one would not have attributed to a -- an HVO unit. But it is not impossible that if that was the point of effort in July that a collection of HVO equipment was heading that way, but again it seems more likely this is a formed military unit with a range of weaponry, particularly the multi-barrel rocket launcher, which was coming from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn the page and look at paragraph 6, and this is the, I take it, SpaBat sector. Under Mostar the second paragraph it says, "Up to 15 military vehicles without -- without vehicle registration numbers were observed parked in Ljubuski," and the comment, "the removal of licence place has often been used by the HVO to disguise the presence of HV troops in Bosnia." Can you comment on that? Had you come across that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly some of the vehicles that I observed in January had licence plates removed, but at that time there seemed to be little pretense because there was an indication on the side of the cabs that it was HV forces. But, yes, the removal of licence plates was, I think, probably a rather superficial attempt to cover what was there, but it wasn't unheard-of. I came across and heard of this practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just before stepping off paragraph 4 on that same page, under the same section it says, "A SpaBat platoon observed 15 truckloads of civilians, mainly women and children and old people travelling from Ljubuski to Grude." Did you have any knowledge of such movements of population?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We regularly heard of movements of civilian population both out, as I referred to yesterday, out of Central Bosnia, but this, because it's SpaBat and SpaBat's based in Mostar, it's difficult to draw any conclusions. This could simply be the movement of displaced persons who had come in. It could be relocation. But, yes, movement of civilians in large numbers on trucks and buses was something that I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And then just for the record, if you look at paragraph 1 under that same section, we just note that there's reference to heavy shelling of Muslims in areas of the city, and that is in Mostar, I take it. Were you aware of any shelling in Mostar at that stage, even if it wasn't your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and experienced it myself later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can look at Exhibit 06448. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's titled CC Mostar, 5 November 1993. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I wrote this document, although my name isn't at the end. As a matter of interest, I always put my name at the end but I don't know why they're being cut off here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And just for the information of the Court that these documents were provided -- when they were provided by the provider certain actions were made within them, and that could explain for that. Sir, if we can look at the section, Military, on the first page, and if we can look at the second paragraph thereof. M1 which is changed to M4 by somebody, "reported sighting six buses from Osijek carrying soldiers with HVO and HV markings. UNPROFOR report 15 buses with the same passengers on route Triangle heading for Prozor." Do you have any comments on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not sure who made the amendments although obviously after "transmission," it says, "corrected by HCC." That's not so important. What we are clearly stating is that a team observed buses from Osijek, which of course is in Croatia, carrying soldiers with HVO and HV markings. So they are also noting that they're heading up route Triangle. So from Herzegovina up to the front line of Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's step off this document. Now, yesterday you described to the Chamber how you came across an HV unit on route Triangle during January, and if we can look at Exhibit 07625. 07625. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is a weekly summary for the week 14 to 20 January 1994, issued by headquarters in Zagreb. Could you perhaps just comment on the origins or the status of this kind of report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the headquarters of ECMM based in Zagreb was required to produce a weekly information sheet which was sent to the contributing countries. This is being produced by the info and analysis cell, so there would be monitors compiling this report from sources in the field, including those from regional centre Zenica, and of course regional centre Zenica would have been fed with its reports by the coordination centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if you can turn to page 4 of this document, and I want you to have a look at specifically paragraphs 14 to 16. And this describes while travelling on route Triangle HRC Zenica and HCC Mostar witnessed the move of approximately 30 vehicles. Is this the report of your sighting which you had referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you have any views at that time regarding the presence of HV troops in this area in relation to the proximity of peace talks that were due?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- well, this for me was the moment at which I suspended any disbelief, although I had seen those reports and we just referred to one way back in July where we have UNPROFOR stating it. This is the first time I saw it myself and had no doubt that I was seeing a formed military unit that was not from HVO forces. Moving up -- I was coming from Central Bosnia with the head of the regional centre, so I was travelling south-west. This convoy we had to get on the side of the road for it to pass. It was heading up to the front line at Prozor. When you look at what we observed, multi-barrel rocket launchers, both vehicle and towed, and 422-millimetre mortars, towed artillery, one could only assume that this was a unit that had firepower and potential offensive capability. There had been speculation for some time, as I said earlier, of there being some sort of thrust by HVO up into -- into middle Bosnia. Although our assessment was that was very unlikely unless there were other forces introduced that altered the equation that had led to the stability of the front lines, and this could be it. It was either to achieve that military aim or to send signals to politicians at a moment where there were discussions going on, and of course we're talking here now about the time of the Washington Agreement, and it was either to send signals of power and capability or, in the event of perhaps failed negotiations, to actually go for seizing land and gaining as much as could be gained through military force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned that during a meeting with General Praljak he had indicated to you that the presence of HV troops in Herceg-Bosna was only due to people volunteering, and therefore these weren't people who were sent down there. Can you comment on that explanation of his in light of this unit that you saw on route Triangle during January 1994?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his explanation had a ring of credibility about it in terms of it was very likely that soldiers return from HV to fight with HVO, but this was different. This was a formed HV military unit and would not have been purely manned by Bosnian Croats returning from HV army. This was an HV Croatian army unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's turn to document or Exhibit 07 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to the previous document. Could -- could we look at document 15, please -- sorry, paragraph 15. It states that, "someone from the UNPROFOR, 5th Brigade, on the side of a vehicle." What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've made -- I've made the comment that it could be referencing 5 HV Guards Brigade, and then I go on to state where that brigade is normally stationed, garrisoned in Vinkovci, which is in -- was in Sector East. In Croatia but in UN territory designated Sector East. We saw the writing, "5 Brigade." It was my interpretation that this could be 5 HV Guards Brigade. I was in little doubt, sir, as I mentioned earlier that this was a -- this was an HV unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, it's -- if we turn to Exhibit -- just the next document, Exhibit 07652. 07652. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, this is stated to be a weekly summary for the period 16 to 22 January, 1994. Could you comment on this document, the origins?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This has come out of headquarters in Zagreb and would again be a compilation and some analysis of the situation over that week, as extracted from the reports sent by the various teams in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 3, paragraph 11. It says, "more HVO troops than necessary," and then the second sentence, "there is also increased evidence of Croatian HV involvement in the vicinity. Certainly groups of officers with HV insignia and a convoy of vehicles have been sighted." Is this a reference to the same sighting you had made or could it be a different unit?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is probably the one that I referred to, but I couldn't be -- it's formed within that timeframe but it could equally be another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: For interest, paragraph 13 and the same page, and here we see a significant development in Mostar was the replacement of Mate Boban by Akmadzic. Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, previously we'd been speculating about the future of Mate Boban, and we had believed that it was a condition being placed by the international community on Croatia, for the delivery of any peace settlement required Mate Boban's departure. When I went to the Presidency meeting on the 29th of December, there had been discussion there by Ivo Lozancic. He mentions that the uncertainty about the leadership was causing issues and by this date it appears that Mate Boban has gone and Mr. Mile Akmadzic had -- had taken over, and Mile Akmadzic had been at the time of the 29th of December the international relations minister and had been representing the Bosnian Croat perspective at those talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kruger, would you allow me a technical point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Watkins, we have now had two weekly reports. One covers the week from 14 January to 20 January, and the other covers 16 January to 22nd January. They're both from HQ ECMM Zagreb, and they largely overlap. Could you explain this? It's a bit striking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour, appear a little unusual, and, as any person in the field will say, headquarters always do operate in a slightly unusual way. I would -- I think, sir, to answer your question fully, could I go back to the other document and just see, because there were various elements within the headquarters. One previously was from the -- I think it was a milinfo summary, and this may well have come out of another element. It may be a more political focus than a military focus, but if I can just go back to the other one I might be able to bring a bit more clarification to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Someone is going to have to remind me what the number was of the previous one. Was it this one before? Yeah, okay. I don't think I can give you a satisfactory explanation, sir, for it, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour Judge Trechsel, you ask about 14 January to 20 January. I think that we ought to add into the transcript that it is 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. They both are the same year, of course, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- for confusion later on in analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we may turn to Exhibit 07614.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I might just offer one perhaps small insight. It could be that if we look at the distribution, the distribution may give us a clue. The distribution of the first team -- sorry, the first report, that is 7625, is actually to the other regional centres and not, as I stated earlier, going off to the member countries, and it could be that this was the first one that was pushed out to those regional centres and the second one may have a different distribution, a different audience, and may have been slightly refined. That's a -- just a possible explanation, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, Exhibit 07614. This document says it is a daily monitoring activity report of 17 January 1994. Could you just comment on the origins of this report.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters in addition to producing that weekly summary, which involved a little bit more analysis, did a daily report, and this is -- this is one of those -- an example of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to two things in this report. On page 2, paragraph 10. And this was Mr. Humo, deputy commander of the BiH brigade, "told ECMM that HVO was concentrating forces in Mostar west with both Bosnian Croat HVO and Croatian HV soldiers. He said that if the Geneva talks failed, the Muslims would be expecting a major attack." Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think this was broadly in line with what I said earlier. There was a show of force, and how that force was to be used was twofold. It was either to send political signals of capability or actually to take territory in the event of a failure of political discussions, and Mr. Humo was repeating something which General Budakovic, the commander of 4th Corps based in Mostar, had been telling us for some while including when we took the -- Ambassador de Baenst to meet him. He was very specific about HV units there are location so what we're seeing here is reinforcing of that but with an explanation as to why and linking it definitively to the talks in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we'd quickly look at the next paragraph. We needn't spend much time on this. This is just a report that ECMM team Siroki Brijeg, "their car was targeted by 6 or 7 rounds of heavy machine-gun fire while crossing the bridge to get into Mostar east," and then, what's interesting, "the targeting without doubt HVO was deliberate." Could you comment on this, and did this kind of thing happen on other occasions, too, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were sniped at in our armoured vehicles as we travelled from West Mostar into East Mostar on a not irregular basis. What was important about this was, this is heavy calibre. This is 12.7 machine-gun. A -- AK47 rifle round will bounce off the car and just make a little clang. A 12.7 will go straight through. So the fact that one of my vehicles had been targeted by this heavy calibre weapon, and there were two ex-military members on board, meant that I had credibility in their explanation as to where the rounds had come, and as a result of this I made direct complaints to the HVO military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you remember to whom you made these complaints?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was to Bozo Raguz, who was a liaison officer in operational zone Mostar headquarters in West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you recall what his reaction was?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I made the complaint because it was important to make the complaint, but I never anticipated that it would bring any major changes. It was the same with freedom of movement and, again, not just with Bosnian Croats. Whenever we had our operations interrupted, we made a point of bringing it to the attention of the authorities of whoever had caused us problems but it sometimes resulted, if it was freedom of movement, in temporary lifting of those restrictions, but one knew that an event like this could well be repeated and as a result we slightly changed our operational activity. I didn't allow any single vehicles to go into East Mostar after this. We always sent two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can turn to Mostar itself. Can you tell the Court, during your period as HCC or head of the CC Mostar, what was the status of the conflict? How would you describe the status of the conflict you found there as either defensive or offensive with regard to the various sides?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the front line really from Prozor down through Jablanica and down through East Mostar was static but active. I mean, there were continual and constant skirmishing, was firing of artillery, but the firing of artillery was massively one way. There were and we observed some occasional mortar rounds coming out of East Mostar to West Mostar, but consistently daily, and witnessed by myself, we had shellings by HVO forces into East Mostar. They would be regular and daily occurrences. It wasn't a continual bombardment. It would be three or four rounds dropping without any warning, of course, and then, you know, a period when there wasn't any, and then again later. So it was persistent, demoralising, and caused casualties. And as an addition to the explanation I gave earlier about the circumstances in East Mostar, wounded could only be treated in the hospital in East Mostar, and again that would contrast with anyone who was wounded in West Mostar. They would have been able to be evacuated and ultimately go to hospital facilities in -- in Croatia or elsewhere. In East Mostar you stayed in East Mostar. You went to the hospital in East Mostar, and if you're lucky you came out of East Mostar hospital alive. I went to that hospital and I saw the conditions, and they were awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you ever stay over in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Overnight?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't normal for monitoring activity to take place after dark, which of course meant many limitations because movement after dark would not be observed by us. However, we -- I did myself stay in East Mostar on a number of occasions overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what your experience or your general experience was when you did this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a -- we lived -- lived, I stayed in damaged houses with no water, with no electricity, and with the anxiety of and actually hearing detonations ongoing. Not continuous, but just sporadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know what kind of weaponry the shelling of East Mostar was being conducted by or with?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily it was with mortar rounds and also with some tank rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: As a former artillery officer, could you perhaps provide the Court with a few insights as to the effect of shelling into a built-up area with mortars and with tanks?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery is an indirect and what's called an area weapon. It is not a particularly precise weapon, whereas a tank is a precise shell that is fired and in a direct mode. So -- without lapsing into too much military-speak, artillery fire and mortar fire is done indirectly. In other words, the people firing the weapon don't necessarily have to see the target. It is either just fired into a general area or it is observed by someone separate from the firing unit who will then adjust the artillery to have the effect, but it is not a weapon that is used to, for instance, take out a single building. It would be used to hit an area. So it was -- it's indiscriminate. And the nature of an artillery round or a mortar round is one of detonation and fragmentation to create as much shrapnel as possible and as much damage as possible. And that is distinct from a round fired from a tank where the target is observed by those firing the weapon and the nature of the ammunition is one of penetration, largely, rather than detonation and fragmentation, although there are some rounds fired from a tank to achieve that. But it's -- it's indiscriminate and 120-millimetre is a serious thing that you don't want to get on the wrong end of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've mentioned tank fire, and you said that the goal was penetration, and prior to that you said that usually there is an observer. Well, I have a technical question. When a tank fires, in order for this fire to be precise, is there another weapon that would shoot first so that the tank be able to adjust the precision of the fire? A light weapon, for example? Would there be this mechanism with the tracing bullet which would hit the target which would enable the spotter in the tank to see what is happening? Is that a technique that's used when tanks fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, although my speciality isn't tanks. That is a technique which is used on tanks and also on some anti-tank weapons used by the infantry, that there is a ranging round fired by a low calibre weapon and once the target is marked on that, the calibration on the main weapon will -- will match that and there will be a hit. That system now is largely redundant and been replaced by lasers, which will give you the same accurate information without actually firing a round. But it is also employed in some shoulder launched anti-tank weapons. Certainly the British Army has those, where the first round that the soldier will fire will be to ensure that he has the correct range and site setting, and when he's confident that he has, he will fire the main armament. If I could just add one clarification. When I was talking about the observer, that is primarily in connection with mortars and with artillery. It is the observer that is guiding the gun that is firing. You -- you don't very often have an observer associated with tank fire. It is the commander in the tank and the gunner in the tank who are doing the observing, and they're seeing the target and they're firing directly at the target. The advantage of the artillery firing indirectly is that it can be a long way away, over hills, hidden, and doesn't have to disclose itself to the target, whereas a tank firing directly at a target, even with concealment, is going to be in view of that target. It has to see that target, and therefore it is a target itself if the capability exists to hit that tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have stood up to ask for the floor for a technical question, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think the witness understood your question with respect to when a tank opens fire. I think that you asked that whether before the first tank shell was fired at any time or any place, whether from the tank or anti-aircraft gun, and this was referred to by a witness, whether the target was fired at and whether that would be a way in which a tank could be more precise in the firing. I don't think that exists anywhere at all, but I'll let the witness answer. The tank is an autonomous device, so you can tell us with sights, 12.7 millimetres or 20 millimetres, a smaller calibre, can you target a target with a tank shell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the purpose of my question. It seems to me that you did answer the question, but could you perhaps answer the question that was just put forward by Mr. Praljak, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that Mr. Praljak's question, Your Honour, is the same as yours, and I do repeat that it is a known technique for tanks to have two calibre weapons, a small calibre that might be 12.7, .50, 7.62, alongside, and in it's -- attached to the tank as well as its main armour, and that the smaller round can be fired as a range finder before firing the main tank. That wouldn't always be the case, and tank battles tend to be fast, but that is a technique used by tank units. They would fire from their own tank a small calibre weapon that would then give them the range and sureness that when they fired the large-calibre weapon it would hit the target. An older rather than a modern technique but it definitely happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the other generals would like to speak. Perhaps it would be preferable to wait until the -- wait until later. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to present the following position, and that is that this witness is not telling us correctly how the tanks operate. It can have a 12.7 machine-gun or 7.62, but it is for close -- fighting close, close up. Now, what about if you have a bullet that is 7.62 calibre, how can you determine the distance if you use this type of calibre bullet? A tank is very powerful. It has the possibility for autonomous viewing. And I'd like to ask the witness that if you have an attack of 20 tanks or 50 tanks in one area how you determine a target. So what I wanted to say is that the witness is not well-versed in the subject matter of tanks and how they work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think we must continue because it's becoming extremely technological from a military point of view and there will be other witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, if we may turn to the second last document in the binder, Exhibit 09997. 09997. And this is another daily report or a daily sitrep dated the 20th of December, 1993. Could you just comment once again briefly on the origins or status of this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report coming from the EC liaison officer based in Kiseljak in the UNPROFOR headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you look at page 2 of the document, the fourth paragraph, entitled Southern BH Command. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It says, "A Mostar -- an active day in Mostar. SpaBat patrols reported 26 incoming and five outgoing mortar rounds in East Mostar. SA fire and HMG exchange continued throughout the day." Could you perhaps just briefly comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. SA is small-arms fire. HMG is heavy machine-gun exchanges. That is an indication that the rounds weren't all going one way but it gives a good example of the sort of relative weight. There are 26 incoming, and SpaBat was based in Mostar, so that is coming in from HVO,, and the five outgoing are armija rounds being fired into West Mostar. In terms of the numbers and the weight, this would be in my estimation at the higher end of a day's activity. There were counts, and I think if one referred to all the SpaBat reports you'd be able to get a very clear picture of the amount, but if helps the Court my impression would be that we would be seeing and hearing probably half that number. Let's say between somewhere between about 10 rounds a day would be an average day in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Would that be during the period that you were CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the period that I can personally vouch to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just very briefly. On the next page, right at the bottom, D, and if we recall that release from detainees from HVO detention centres was going on, it seems that here we still have a further report on such releases, and with SpaBat involvement.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you just point me more specifically to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The next page, D.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you have any comments on that paragraph? That you had written 15 detainees released and SpaBat involvement and ICRC from Rodoc?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, checking the date 20th of December so we're very much into, in fact towards the end, I think, of the release of prisoners by HVO unilateral as declared by Mate Boban and as delivered in terms of activity by Mr. Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've -- you've described the conditions that you encountered in East Mostar. Were there any attempts by the international community to establish the actual population in East Mostar during the period that you were head of CC Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This would have been largely -- well, it was of interest to us all but particularly to UNHCR who would be providing humanitarian aid and would need to have as much detail as they could on numbers. The numbers, however, were always notoriously inaccurate. I mean, clearly because we're in war conditions, there was difficulty in any civilian administration, and in those conditions having an accurate record, but there were various figures that were mooted and used, if you like as -- in order to steer the amount of humanitarian aid that went to an area. In the case of East Mostar, the figures ranged dramatically. I think the highest figures I heard were -- were probably in the 50.000 range I think more likely it was somewhere between 30 and 40, but that's -- that's a guess on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, if we can look at Exhibit 0995 -- 09995. Sorry, Triple 9, 5. That's my mistake. 09995. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's another daily sitrep dated the 23rd of December, 1993. Would you have also known or contributed to this sitrep?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the information for this sitrep would actually be coming from the UN forces. It's the liaison officer sitting in UNPROFOR who is looking at their reports and extracting information from their reports to inform us, rather than our reports being -- forming the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What I would like to direct your attention to is the third page of this document, and it's the fourth page in the B/C/S version. There's a paragraph dated -- numbered number 4, southern BH command right at the bottom of the page, and towards the end of that little paragraph there's report of snipe activity, but then there's reference to the "planned escort of BritFor trucks transporting the field hospital into East Mostar on 23 December," which is cancelled. Do you have any knowledge or recollection of this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a field hospital donated by, I believe, one of the Nordic countries, and it was destined initially for, I believe, Konjic. It was held in Ploce for a long time, and the movement of this field hospital to Konjic didn't happen, and then at some stage I think the decision was made that it would go to East Mostar. Getting this field hospital into the area of need proved to be very, very difficult and over a fairly prolonged period there were attempts to -- to deploy it, and I don't actually remember that ever being successful, though it is possible that it -- that it was after the period I left as HCC Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, we're going to turn now to a number of documents just recording the release of detainees from the HVO detention centres. Looking at the same document you have, page 11 thereof, and actually if you look in the top right-hand corner it would be the one numbered R0213946, 3946. In the B/C/S version it would be page 10. Now, sir, there's a paragraph numbered 8, Humanitarian Activity, and just the first part of that detainees released -- the release operation. "Today SpaBat and ICRC again successfully evacuated 160 detainees from Rodoc." Do you have anything to add to that or any comments?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the continuation of the releases that we referred to earlier, and Rodoc is also sometimes referred to as the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Exhibit 06590. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's a report, daily report, by CC -- from CC Mostar dated 11 November 1993. Is this your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my report. I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it mentions, if we turn to paragraph 5 on the second page, Humanitarian, and if we look at paragraph 3 of that, in the B/C/S version it's page 2, in the middle, "M1 met Semir Boskailo in Konjic hospital. He said he had been taken prisoner in Dretelj before release in October 1993. He claimed that prisoners were hidden from ICRC when they visited camps so a complete register could not be made." Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I could add anything significantly to that. I think it was always difficult, certainly for us as a monitors and from the ICRC to get a complete picture. You're going into a controlled environment, and you don't necessarily have access to all buildings, and so this is possible, and I think historically we will have seen it in other areas, and -- and -- but I can't add any more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if we turn to the first page of that document, under Political, "HCC," that's you, "met with Smail Klaric," who is described as the president of the War Presidency Mostar, and in the middle of that paragraph it states, there's reference of, "Mostar county had recently formed on 7 November in Mostar and had authority over the municipalities of Stolac, Capljina, Mostar, Jablanica." Could you perhaps briefly comment on what this relates to or what this is?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. ECMM was dealing in many issues and issues but perhaps where it had a unique lead was on political structures, hence my interest in the formation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. But equally we were discovering and encountering commentary from armija, that they were re-organising their civilian structures along a county basis, and we did see a number of personalities begin to -- to change, and they were telling us that they were part of the new structure. So when I first went to East Mostar as head of the coordination centre, I was meeting another person whose name I'm sorry I can't remember, but Smail Klaric soon became the main interlocutor, along with Ibrahim Kaluda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Very briefly, I don't know whether you would have any comment on that, but Stolac and Capljina were areas included within the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Could you comment on the fact that they are also then included in this Mostar county for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that simply is because the Muslims did not recognise the boundaries as identified by CRHB and were simply -- whether they actually physically held the territory was not so important -- well, it was important to them but their political boundaries would go over the military front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Before stepping on to the next document, if I may just briefly refer back to the mobile hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, one point of clarification. The gentleman indicated that the army -- that the armija, that is the army of ABiH, was restructuring their civilian structures. I wonder if the gentleman misspoke. But here we have the military restructuring the civilian structures. Is that what the gentleman indicated? It's on page 28. I don't have the exact line. It might have just gone off the page. It's on line 23, 24 of page 28. "Armija was restructuring the civilian structure," and is that what the gentleman wanted to indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I think you're right to draw attention to a probably rather clumsy speak there. I have throughout the -- given -- giving my evidence sometimes referred to Bosnian Muslims, sometimes referred to armija, sometimes referred to BiH. I did not mean in this case mean to suggest that it was the military re-organising the civilian. It was a civilian structure which was being developed. Its origin was coming out of the Sarajevo government and indeed Ibrahim Kaluda was the coordination for Mostar, but actually I believe he was, if you like, an emissary from Sarajevo. So it was a political development and not one by the armija forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, just briefly back to the mobile hospital which was then scheduled to go into East Mostar, what were -- what were the actual difficulties or the problems involved in get it in? What prevented the hospital going into East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's most obvious point it was freedom of movement. There would be a -- a physical restriction. The vehicles carrying these containers - and I think there was something like 30 or 40 containers - were not physically allowed to move but of course the -- it's, why were the barriers there in the first place? That would have been a political decision, and it would have been a decision not made in isolation from other humanitarian activity, other activity generally. There were always linked issues. One could never seemingly deal with a specific issue. It always had to be related to another. There was always an attempt for some sort of -- of balance, and therefore that is why, for instance, when we were referring earlier to the attempt to evacuate hospitals, it was happening in Nova Bila, a Croatian -- a Bosnian Croat hospital at the same time as the East Mostar hospital, so there was always linkages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you know who from the Bosnian Croat side would have been involved in moving these -- this hospital or preventing it from moving?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Bosnian Croat forces wouldn't have been involved in its actual movement but it's -- it's prevention of movement could only have come from the highest level. This would not have been a local command decision and it would either be the highest level militarily or politically. So in terms of names this would require Mate Boban, senior members of the government, or senior members of the HVO. I -- I couldn't state specifically where that specific decision sat, but it would either be with, at this time, November, General Praljak, Ante Roso, we're at a changeover point here. It could have involved Jadranko Prlic. It would certainly have involved Mate Boban. And if I had to make an estimate or a judgement, it would be Mate Boban's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, if we can look at Exhibit 04431. 04431. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's described as an ECMM report number 34 for 22 to 29 August 1993. Could you tell the Court first of all, what does it mean, "ECMM humanitarian activity report"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- during its various evolutions and iterations, the ECMM had slightly different structures of team activity on the ground, and at one stage it had teams that were specifically dealing and only dealing with humanitarian issues, and we had another unit that was dealing with airfield monitoring, and then we had the general teams. By the time we get to August 1993, in fact, the functions are really being carried out which the generalist teams. So we don't see a specific humanitarian team. But the importance of the humanitarian activity was recognised, and so a cell was formed in the headquarters whose job it was to comb through every report from whatever source and extract anything which had a humanitarian connection, and they would write a -- a report, and this is one of those reports coming out of the headquarters at Zagreb of the humanitarian cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Would you have also seen this report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It had a wide distribution. I -- I can't say that I specifically saw this one unless we go through it a little bit more and something leaps out, but we had those reports coming out of the headquarters, and I did read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to paragraph 29 of the report. And this is the section entitled Prisoners and Detainees.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the second paragraph of that -- sorry, no. Paragraph 29. "On 29 August, team 3, Medjugorje, reported that ICR assume the conditions in the detention camps Dretelj and Gabela to be much worse than in Rodoc camps they visited. Access to the two camps can't be achieved before ICRC have visited the Muslims camps on the east bank of Mostar." Can you comment on what is reported here?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's recognising that ICRC had the lead in terms of visiting detention camps, and we're reporting what they're telling us. So it's not -- it's not an ECMM experience but what it's saying here is, it's pointing out, again, as I mentioned earlier, a linkage that it appears they are reporting they are prevented from gaining access to Dretelj and Gabela at that time until they have demonstrated to the HVO that there is equal access to their HVO forces that were held by armija in East Mostar. So it's that linkage issue again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to paragraph 33. "On 26 August, team V2 Gornji Vakuf observed in Trnovaca 25 prisoners of war civilian internees digging trenches close to the front line." Did you ever come across any instances of labour by detainees?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was something which happened and was observed both armija forces making HVO dig -- or captives dig trenches, but I personally saw and witnessed a Muslim being required to dig trenches by HVO, but this was in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you ever come across this mentioned as an issue when you eventually became head of Mostar CC?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had allegations made again from both sides that civilians were used as human shields. They were used to carry out dangerous front line activity, and so it was an issue that was -- we discussed with -- with both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Paragraph 34. The same team on 26 August met the mayor of Capljina, and he also said, "the municipality has released a number of Muslim men from a camp, but the rest would be kept for later prisoner of war exchanges." Do you know what that was about? Do you recall such an event?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this predates the Mate Boban initiative, but it was a constant theme throughout the period that I was in Bosnia to try and -- and release prisoners, so it appears here that we do have an initiative at some level that has been successful, but clearly it isn't a complete evacuation of that camp but a statement that some are being held for, if you like, bargaining, again something both sides did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you comment on the fact that the mayor of Capljina in this instance appears to have a hand in the release of detainees from -- from a camp? And my comment -- I'd like you to comment from the point of view of how can this be in light of other existing structures which may be in place for such matters.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there would have to be -- this couldn't be an initiative with the mayor of Capljina carried out in -- of his own volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If the mayor of Capljina says that the municipal structures took part in that, then we must believe him. Now, what my learned colleague is putting to the witness, I think, is entering the realm of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Also, there's the lack of foundation. If you look at the beginning of the answer, "this could not be an initiative with the mayor." So it begs the question, at whose initiative was this? Does he know for a fact keeping in mine the date and place the gentleman was at that point in time, in country, that is. So unless there is a foundation it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond. I think that the question is -- is justified in the sense of the witness was in the area at the time. He had gained experience of the personalities involved, the people in various positions, and therefore he is qualified to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're talking about a specific incident, Your Honour, not in general. He's asking him about a specific incident. So he must lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards what was just described about the mayor, you said that the mayor of Capljina -- you mentioned the mayor of Capljina. Did you actually see him and speak to the mayor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. At the time of this report, which is the 26th of August, I was in Central Bosnia. I can answer more generally if it helps about structures, and that was where I was lead to go in my answer, but I don't know whether I'm allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On this -- on this instance, Your Honour, I suggest that he not be answering the question unless a proper foundation can be laid. Based on the answer the gentleman has no personal knowledge. Whether in general something happened or not, that's irrelevant. The Prosecution is -- is pointing to a specific incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stated that the mayor of Capljina -- in fact, you didn't see him because you were elsewhere but you added that you could talk about the structure of the municipality. Have you studied those structures? Why is it that you affirm that you can talk about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I believe I do have an understanding of the civil and military structures, and what is important is, is how those contrasted between what was happening in Herzegovina and what was happening in Central Bosnia. I was going to say that in Central Bosnia, because of the isolated nature of pockets of minority groups, it was quite possible for an individual to actually -- and often a mayor, and I could give you an example of Zepce or Vares, where a mayor would have authority and would be able to carry out independent actions. My comment would simply be that in Herzegovina that independence of initiative at a political level was not achievable because there was a control structure there. In other words, they may be given some latitude to do some local arrangements, but if that was to extend beyond what was politically acceptable there was a means of -- of checking that individual authority. Up in Central Bosnia there was no means of checking that individual authority. So all I was going to say with reference to Capljina, Capljina fell within Herzegovina. Herzegovina, there was a contiguous land area controlled by the Bosnian Croat forces, and the mayor of Capljina would not have been able to act completely independently of the political structures in Mostar. He would have some latitude but not complete independence. The mayor of Zepce would have a lot more independence, if that helps I sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, there's a lack of foundation. There hasn't been -- and I can cover this on cross-examination with additional time, but what the gentleman hasn't answered is how has he studied the structure in Bosnia-Herzegovina. How does he know exactly what is happening at this particular time and the actual powers of this particular mayor. That's -- so anecdotally, he can say, in general, yes, this might be the case, but, specifically, how does he know? And that's the point. He's trying to make a difference between what's happening in Central Bosnia, in Herzegovina, and he's trying to show somehow in Herzegovina you have a parastate in existence where the municipality's under total control. Now, he needs to lay a foundation. Has he studied? Has he looked at the legislation in order to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Your Honour, this is for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- to see what powers exactly the mayor has vis-a-vis the other structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, sir, you have distinguished between Herzegovina and Central Bosnia, and everyone can read the transcript to that effect, but that distinction, that is, as regards the relationship between the municipal structures and their scope of action and responsibility and their position vis-a-vis the military forces, what exactly enables you draw those conclusions? Have you made personal observations? Did colleagues report to you? What is it that enables you to draw those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Experience on the ground, Your Honour, in terms of what was possible achieve as a monitor and how one achieved that. We operated in a different way in Central Bosnia. We may well have had a command structure, be it armija or military -- sorry, be it armija or HVO, but one didn't necessarily in Central Bosnia solve a situation by going to the person who appeared to be the senior commander. So in my previous evidence when I've been to the Tribunal, I have noted that one would possibly resolve in some areas in Central Bosnia an issue by reference to the authority, the power, where the power lay in that particular locality and not necessarily by having to go to the senior military or political leader in Central Bosnia. My experience in Herzegovina was different. My experience in Herzegovina was that an issue in, let's say, Tomislavgrad or Siroki Brijeg are a major issue, could equally be dealt with at a senior level in Mostar, because those people in Mostar had a connection and had an ability to influence the activities of military and civil structures in Herzegovina that they didn't have over Central Bosnia or that in Central Bosnia commanders had over all of the pockets in isolation. I have met many of the mayors myself. First of all, when I was a monitor in Tomislavgrad, I would have seen the mayor of Tomislavgrad, Jablanica, Gornji Vakuf, and so on, and by the time I came in as HCC of Mostar, and you will have seen by my references to documents yesterday I met many political leaders as well as military leaders, and so over time I built up an impression of what sort of authority and what sort of structures were in existence and was able to contrast them with my experience in Central Bosnia, but I'm not a legal lawyer, and I anticipate that when we get to cross-examining we'll be dealing with that, some of those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now 10.30. We're going to have a 20-minute break, and we shall resume with the examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resume. The registrar has informed me that the Prosecution still has 40 to 45 minutes. Mr. Kruger, therefore, you have three-quarters of an hour to round up your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think that should be sufficient time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, if we may turn to Exhibit 05959. Exhibit 05959. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is an ECMM or CC daily summary -- CC Mostar daily summary of 19 October, 1993. Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I had just arrived in Mostar. It was either the 17th or 19th, I forget exactly. I don't believe this is one that I wrote though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we turn to the second page, at the very top, and in the B/C/S version, that is page 2, the paragraph marked C, I think. Now, it says HCC designate, that would be you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And it says you attended a joint commission formed to discuss humanitarian issues, and then it goes on to describe what happened at this meeting where the media apparently appeared. Do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In whose meeting was this office -- in whose office was this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't actually remember which office it was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can you remember with whom it was specifically?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was supposed to be a joint commission, but there were no BiH representatives there, so it would have been Mr. Bozic, and actually I would have expected that it was -- that Mr. Pusic might have been there, but only Mr. Bozic is mentioned at the moment, and Slobodan Bozic was the deputy minister of defence and also dealing with international relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what happened at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian television came in to -- to film what was going on, and what was going on, of course, were a number of international organisations including the ECMM in discussions with members of the Bosnian Croat commission about humanitarian issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, your assessment on the fact that the BiH representatives were not present, did you have any views on that at the time?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as it was a joint commission, certainly those joint commissions that have been established in Gornji Vakuf and Busovaca reflected or had membership from both Muslim and Croat authorities here. The joint commission didn't have any representatives from the BiH, and the interpretation which we can see later on is that the message -- the presence of the television there was going to be signalling to the audience watching that television of H -- of Bosnian Croat forces working with and cooperating with the international community, and this was something which was regularly raised by military and political leaders, that they felt - the Bosnian Croat political leaders - that they didn't get good international coverage, that the coverage is always biased, one-sided, that it always saw the Muslims as the victims and not the Croats as the victims. It underplayed atrocities where the victims were Croats. For instance, Uzdol. It emphasised things like Stupni Do massacre but didn't seem -- sorry, Uzdol was actually a massacre of Bosnian Croats, and they felt, for instance - that was one example given to me that - that didn't receive the same coverage that Stupni Do had. So there was this continual concern, and I felt that this was probably a message about, you know, cooperation with the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to the next page of this document at the very top, and in the B/C/S version this would be page 4 under paragraph 6, and it says HCC and HCC designate. That would once again be you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And Jesus Amatriain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And it says that this morning you were visiting the HVO headquarters in Citluk, requesting -- requested by HRC and CC Herceg Novi in order to get a letter of guarantee for a cease-fire. And then you say the letter had already been done. And then in the comment, "Due to the fact that General Petkovic was not in Citluk we were talking to Colonel Akrap." Could you perhaps just elaborate on this, give the Court some insight into this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just take a moment to read that whole paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't throw a lot of light on this. I can say that I didn't write this. This does not have my use of language here. What I can say is that this clearly was an issue that we were trying to resolve, and it required an agreement at a level beyond that that could be achieved at CC Mostar, hence the involvement of the regional centre and also the team -- and there was one ECMM team based in Montenegro, and the issue here is about power -- power supply, and it required obviously coordination between the various -- that would be Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs. I -- I don't recall any more detail. The comment is, as I say, not my comment, but it's just noting here that we didn't see General Petkovic. We saw his -- his assistant, Colonel Akrap, and I don't believe that I saw General Petkovic at all in this -- in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, just a few final things or one final thing on the issue of release of detainees. You have mentioned a few times already that Mate Boban made or issued a unilateral instruction for the release of detainees from HVO detention centres. My question to you is had you had any prior indication that something like this was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember -- not specifically a unilateral. Certainly and almost continually there was an attempt by ICRC to broker large-scale release of -- coordinated release of prisoners of war or -- by both sides at the same time. That had, as we've seen before, had some small and local successes but not done at a large level. What Mate Boban's statement was, was a very clear statement and a good move in terms of sending the right signals to the international community that regardless of cooperation and linkages, he was going to release prisoners from -- from the detention centres. So those releases, the international community still hoped, would encourage the armija forces to reciprocate, and when they didn't, of course, that gave the Bosnian Croats even more kudos in terms of we're doing it, they're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's have a look at Exhibit 07280. 7280. You have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, this is a report from CC -- daily report from CC Mostar dated 20 December 1993. Is this a report by you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 7, the assessment, right at the end of the document and there says the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna image offensive is continuing on the international arena with Mate Boban announcing his expectation of reciprocal prisoner of war release. We've just touched upon this. Do you have anything to add to this comment or assessment?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I've covered it in my previous response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Of course just for the record if we look under Humanitarian, in the first paragraph and the second paragraph I see you're still recording the release of detainees from the various detention centres?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It's part of this Mate Boban programme. It wasn't clearly, as we've established in the last couple of days, a single event. It was a scheduled release with anticipated numbers being given to us at times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can look at the very next document in the binder, that is Exhibit 07286. 07286. Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And this is once again CC Mostar daily summary, dated 21 December 1993, so just the next day from the previous one. Is this your document as well?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, once again if we can turn to the assessment. And your assessment once again focuses on the image war, and you say, "it continues with BiH losing and CRHB are expected to maintain the momentum." And then you go further, one method would be to release the BiH helicopters without maintaining the Croatian Defence Council prisoners of war link, and then, specifically, "it is ironic that in the current climate the CRHB would [as read] present such actions as yet more evidence of their unilateral goodwill." Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
