utterances.text: "CRHB could present such action as yet more evidence." Yeah, my impression was at the time that the Bosnian Croats were beginning to turn around their image. They were not only making gestures, they were actually releasing prisoners, and this was -- this was going down well, and the BiH were not reciprocating, so my comments that CRHB are -- are beginning to win this -- this public relations element. But what was surprising and -- was this continued detaining of the two helicopters, because this had become an issue almost out of all proportion. I mean, it was raised at every level and just about every possible occasion with the right authorities about why it hadn't -- why they hadn't been released why they were still being held, when they were going to be released, and it seemed here I'm making the comment that, you know, a simple gesture of their release would be yet more evidence of the Bosnian Croats actually responding to what the international community was -- was asking and gesturing, but they didn't, or they didn't then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea the -- these two helicopters, what kind of -- how much of the armija or ABiH's airpower did this represent, or air force?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The airfield monitors that I mentioned earlier had given us some impression of -- of forces, and it was our understanding that the armija had four helicopters. So seizing two was instantly holding or neutralising 50 per cent of the air force capability of the armija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can look in the same document. On the first page, under the section Political and the third paragraph thereof, and once again there's reference to John Bryan, and this deals with HVO prisoners being held in Mostar east or the -- and he says, "Armija argue Muslim released so far have been civilians and not soldiers." Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was their stated position and the reason why they would not release the HVO prisoners that they were holding in -- in East Mostar. They said that it should be an exchange of male men -- or men of fighting age, i.e., soldiers, and they hadn't seen soldiers released from Gabela and Ljubuski and Heliodrom and so on. They said that they were saying civilians. And they were only going to hand over soldiers when they saw soldiers being handed over. What I can't comment on is what was the age and gender of those that were released by the HVO to state clearly whether HVO were releasing males of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next document, which is 7290. And this is again a daily summary from CC Mostar, also the 21st of December, 1993. Is this also your document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my document. The reason I hesitate is you pointed out it was the same day, and did we not already send one on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you look at the previous document, which was 7286, I see that that's also the 21st of December, 1993. Could you perhaps comment on two daily summaries on the same day?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be very unusual. I'm just looking at some of the transmission times to see if that's going to give us any clues, and it would appear that if one looks under the UTC time, the document 7286 was transmitted at half past 8.00 on the 22nd of the 12th, 1993. And if we look at the UTC time on document 7290, this was sent at almost 9.00 on the 21st. So what I'm concluding from this is, I got the date wrong on document 7286, and that should in fact be the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. So turning then to 7290. If we can look at the second page, and this is under the section, Humanitarian. On -- in the second paragraph of that section it says, "M9 and M2 monitored the delivery of Muslim prisoners of war to East Mostar." And then further down once again, "Armija and Mostar maintain those released are civilians and not soldiers." Would you like to add anything or comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's the same explanation from the armija. What isn't in here and what I can't remember is -- I mean, we monitored them, but I honestly cannot remember what the gender and age profile was. Had I seen that contradicting, I probably would have said that, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can turn to Exhibit 07606. 07606. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is once again a weekly humanitarian activity report for 9 to 15 January, 1994. Can you comment on the origins of this document or who produced it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would have come out of the humanitarian cell in Zagreb, distributed widely, and because it was humanitarian activity report, it would also have been sent outside of the ECMM structures. So it would have gone to ICRC, UNHCR, and because it came out of the headquarters it probably would have gone direct to their headquarters, so Geneva and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to paragraph 28 of this document. Paragraph 28. It's a few pages on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It says, "the ECMM was informed on 10 January that the release of prisoners as announced by Mate Boban was completed," and then certain statistics are provided. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it proved to be inaccurate because there were releases -- oh, no, sorry. 10th of the 1st. Well, it -- I don't remember exactly when it came to an end, but here we have a summary of statistics and a claim that it all was complete, that the camps were empty on the 10th of the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In the middle of that paragraph it refers to remaining prisoners of war in Heliodrom and in Ljubuski. Can you comment on that in the context of releases being completed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to be contradictory. I don't know whether it goes on to explain what the contradiction might be, but in the first sentence it's saying, look, it's all completed and here are the figures, and then in the second sentence it's saying "remaining POWs." So there's a contradiction in there that I can't explain, but I imagine that the conclusion one should draw is that it wasn't completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can now turn to the issue of Stupni Do. The Court has already heard evidence of what occurred on the 23rd of October, 1993. I I'd like to refer you to Exhibit 06211. This is a CC Mostar daily summary, dated 28 October 1993. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it your document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, under paragraph -- the paragraph dealing with Political, the second paragraph -- no, sorry. Yes. "M4 and -- met Ilija Krezo, municipality -- president of municipality of Livno and Mijo Tokic and asked them to comment on the Stupni Do massacre," and then it says, "they were embarrassed and used the excuse of conflicting reports to avoid comment." Could you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the initial reports coming out of the incident the master at Stupni Do were conflicting and the United Nations and ECMM established, as I referred to yesterday, that the action and killings were committed by HVO forces working under Ivica Rajic from Kiseljak, who had gone through Serb-held territory into the Vares pocket. There were conflicting and confusing reports. It's precisely back to the point that I was making earlier about the connection with those isolated pockets and getting information quickly. Now, the international community had a better communication with those isolated pockets so we very quickly established what had happened. And over a period of probably two, three weeks we very quickly found that our version was accepted pretty broadly by Bosnian Croats. Obviously there were some exceptions, but I do remember raising this with Vladislav Pogarcic and with Jadranko Prlic, and there were, I think, an early acknowledgement that this was HVO forces had committed this even if they'd acted independently and not been instructed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can I refer you to the assessment, paragraph 7 on the next page. "The desire of Croatia to establish their international image as victims has suffered the setback of Stupni Do and the blocked Muslim medevac from East Mostar." Could you comment on this perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's this consistent theme that Bosnian Croats felt that their predicament, the situation of Bosnian Croats, was not articulated to the international community. The ECMM were blamed, journalists were blamed, UN were blamed, but references were made to specific incidents where they felt there had been an under-representation. What I'm say here is that, if you're actually trying to change that image, and I do believe there was a genuine attempt to change that image, obviously Stupni Do, and a very clear indication and establishing that it was -- in fact, HVO forces sets this back, and also we had at this period the failed medevac from East Mostar although the medevac had been successfully concluded from Nova Bila. So there were actions on the ground and things happening which made it very difficult for a policy or a strategy of promoting a new image for the Bosnian Croats to gain credibility when these things were happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Just before stepping off this document, if you can go back to the first page, the Political section, the very first paragraph referring to the -- the helicopters, it says it was confirmed -- "UNPROFOR confirmed that these helicopters had flown the published and approved flight path." Was this indeed correct to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge it was correct. It was part of a coordinated, multi-international agency event, and the clearance of the helicopters would have been required by UNPROFOR because they had the no-fly policy. So they -- if they were going to be in the air, it needed UN's authority for this to happen, and this is confirmation from UNPROFOR that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we turn or return to the issue of the meetings on the 31st of October 1993 with Mate Boban and then with Jadranko Prlic. And if I can refer you in this regard to document 06303. 06303. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's your document, CC Mostar daily summary for 31 October 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now if we look at the very first paragraph under Political, and if we look about two-thirds of the way down the first paragraph, it says, "Boban stated that his information on Stupni Do indicated only armija soldiers had been killed." Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mate Boban was one of the last to acknowledge, if he ever did, the reality on the ground, and here is he stating to our head of mission, this is Ambassador de Baenst, with the unusual spelling of the surname, the head of the regional centre is Martin Garrod and HCC is myself and a political advisor who had come down. I forget the name of that political advisor who accompanied the head of mission. So Mate Boban on the 31st is still saying not HVO forces but armija soldiers who committed the murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Witness, is that what you wanted to say? Because it reads different. It says it reads only ABiH soldiers were killed. It refers to the victims, I think. It's not quite the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are right. He is -- I've written here that he stated it was only armija soldiers that had been killed, not that the armija had committed it. You're absolutely right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we turn to the next paragraph or look at the next paragraph halfway down, this is the paragraph dealing with the meeting with Jadranko Prlic, and when Stupni Do was discussed with him had he said that General Petkovic had removed all local commanders and an investigation was under way. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only state that that is what he said and that is what I report, and it is a political leader stating that the senior military commander is carrying out an investigation. It's not an admittance that it was HVO forces but it is I guess at its very least it is an acknowledge that it looks likely and we're taking action to investigate. And more than that, we've removed local commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. The local commanders being referred to here, do you have any idea who that referred to or --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could refer to the commanders actually in the Vares pocket, or it could indeed refer to the commanders who went to the Vares pocket, Ivica Rajic. I forget the name of the military commanders that were in Zepce at the time. Sorry, in Vares at the time, actually, in that brigade. It may come to me later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Before looking at something else here, during your second tour of duty during 1994, did you ever come across Ivica Rajic or his name in any context?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't come across him. I had met him in 1993. In 1994 we may well have come across his name in that we knew by then that he was linked with the mass -- with the massacre. So, yes, I may well have come across his name there, but I certainly didn't meet him in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you discuss him or did he come up during discussions with Tihomir Blaskic during 1994 when Blaskic was chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly met by then General Blaskic in Posusje, and I may well have raised it, but I would -- I would need to be referred to some documents. I can't bring it straight from my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I would have liked to deal with some other aspects of this document, but I think we dealt sufficiently with them yesterday. If we can turn to a final issue that I would like to raise with you, and that is the destruction of the Stari Most bridge --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I -- could I just make one point, and it's just to clarify something. Yesterday, I was uncertain when we did the visit to East Mostar whether it was General Pasalic or General Budakovic who we met, and I see in this report it's confirming it was still Arif Pasalic in command of 4th Corps at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, how did you come to learn of the destruction of the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt it directly from a Danish monitor and a German monitor it. That would be Henrik Villardsen and Helmut Schlecht, who had been in East Mostar meeting with Mr. Smail Klaric at the moment -- on the morning of which the bridge was destroyed. At the time, I was actually in Jablanica to the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what did you do after you had learned of this destruction?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Henrik Villardsen described the impact of the news on the people who were at the -- that he was meeting, which was devastating. He described something which I witnessed myself later. It really emotionally effected, in particular, Mr. Klaric, but others as well. But he also indicated that it had been caught on video and that he had seen the video, and I said we need a copy of that video, and we obtained one in the coming days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: When you obtained the copy, what did you do with that copy of the video?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: After watching it, I processed it up through our logistics chain to headquarters at ECMM. I had contemplated going directly to the BBC with it, but I felt that there was an important document and the best way to put this into the hands of the international community that would be interested in it would be just to observe the obvious chain. So I sent it up to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And did you -- do you know what happen to the video or whether it was wide -- distributed further from thereon?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly signalled to the headquarters the importance of this video that was arriving. I don't know who they distributed it to, to whom they distributed it, but I did myself see it broadcast on BBC at a later stage. I mean, not in the immediate months. I forget, maybe three or four months later, but it got onto international television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, at this stage I would like to show you a clip, and this is from Exhibit 01040, and this exhibit was dealt with, with a previous witness. Now, sir, I'd like to ask you if you look at this clip and obviously it is an edited version from something wider, whether you recognise the images -- not the images, whether you recognise the video itself perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do recognise it, but it is actually -- it does -- it's slightly different to the one that I had in that mine was colour and you're right to point out that this was an edited version because in the one I had I actually saw the destruction of the bridge, and the date on that was the 8th it, and the bridge came down on the 9th. So this has to be an edited version, but it does seem to be taken from the same perspective, i.e., the same observer position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, the other thing that I -- that I notice is that the film that I have has a wider pan. We very much just saw the bridge, and I think that there are wider angle shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. I won't belabour this or go further into this. I would like to refer you to document 6559, Exhibit 06559. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's CC Mostar, daily summary for 9 November 1993. Is this your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we can look at the first paragraph, the first paragraph, "M2 met Smail Klaric." Is this the meeting you that told us previously just before we entered -- looked at the video?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And there we also see the reference to the video of the destruction?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can refer you to paragraph 3 on that page dealing with military, and it says: "Mostar. The artillery attacks on the city, but there are no reports of accompanying infantry activity it." And then the comment is interesting: "The Old Bridge provided a physical means --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that the speakers slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The comment is interesting: "The Old Bridge provided a physical means of east-bank Muslims supplying those holding precariously on to west bank territory. An HVO follow-up assault on these streets would be - would be consistent with action against the bridge. Comment ends." Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could I begin by drawing attention to the general situation, the opening sentence, and again proving I'm human, there would appear to be a date error there where I say that tank fire began on the 9th of November and continued today, whereas this is the 9th of November. I do know we were notified by Budakovic on the 8th that the bridge was being targeted. It was something I subsequently raised with HVO forces. But returning, sir, directly to your question, the comment. This bridge was used as a supply route to armija forces that were holding on to territory on the west bank, a very small sliver of land, and at this stage this quick assessment is suggesting if you're trying to interpret that action of the destruction of the bridge from a military perspective, you might well want to destroy the bridge and therefore prevent resupply, and if you were then going to take military action to take the territory from the armija that were on the west bank you would -- could anticipate that you may see some infantry follow-up. We didn't, and I don't think that later -- main in this report, in the assessment at the end. It didn't seem to be so much a military as a more political act, the destruction of this bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you -- looking at the assessment, could you comment on your -- on the statement there that the Old Bridge could be linked to events in Vares and explained as bloody-minded revenge?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think at that stands particularly good interrogation, that assessment. I can't really now think what the link I was possibly making there. But I go on to say that the consequences of the destruction should not underestimated, and that is something I would most definitely stand by. It had a major impact on the morale of those in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. Perhaps the gentleman would be assisted. When he says "bloody-minded," when it was translated it means -- you know, it was translated as "blood," where I know that the British sometimes use the term "bloody" to mean something else. So perhaps he could elucidate for a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, just to provide clarification on that term, yes, it is a term in the British language just to explain an action out of spite rather than connected with physical spilling of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could we quickly look at document 6511. Exhibit 06511. Do you have the document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is CC weekly report from HCC Mostar for the week 7 to 13 November, 1993. Is this your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you had been notified the day or previously of this, and is this what is reported under Military, "Artillery, mortar tank has been directed against the city with the Old Bridge reported having received several hits"?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's describing the same activity it, but I actually think there is somewhere else a reference to us being very specifically told by Budakovic, and I believe that I read that somewhere during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you do anything as a result of being informed of this?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I raised the issue with Bozo Raguz, a liaison officer at -- in Mostar. I'm pretty sure he was the liaison officer of the operational zone Mostar. I don't remember clearly whether I raised it before or after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can step on quickly to Exhibit 6646. Exhibit 6646. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is CC weekly report from HCC Mostar for the week 7 to 13 November 1993. Is this your report?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If we can look on the -- under the general situation, the second paragraph under that. It says -- it reports the increased artillery and tank fire in Mostar, and it led to the destruction of the Old Bridge. "Motive was more symbolic than strategic."

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you orientate me to the document again? I'm just missing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's on page 1?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And just about where your finger is now, I see.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Got it, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And what is interesting in this is, "the devastation of the bridge was matched by that of emotions with senior civil leaders reduced to tears." Could you perhaps comment on that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's restating my earlier comments that this had a significant and deep emotional -- it elicited a deep emotional reaction from many people, not just the civil leaders, who we met in East Mostar. That bridge meant a lot to them culturally, symbolly -- symbolically, and it had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, would have -- what would your reaction be to the notion that the Muslims could have destroyed the bridge themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation unless a foundation can be laid that the gentleman was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the witness was talking to these leaders. He saw their reaction to the destruction of the bridge, and I'm asking for his comment in the line of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're not suggesting that the people who he spoke with and who had the emotional attachment and what -- obviously felt emotionally disturbed were the ones that actually destroyed it. So that's not the question. The question is whether he has sufficient knowledge to answer that, the question that's being posed. So if the gentleman was there and was able to observe the shelling at that particular the time on the 8th and the 9th, then perhaps he may be willing to -- may be able to answer the question. So I think it calls -- you know, he -- it calls for a fact not in evidence at this point. So he needs to lay a foundation, otherwise he's speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't belabour this point. I'm sure it will come up in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we can turn to Exhibit -- that one we've done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need -- Mr. Kruger, we've used up five hours. I think we need to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If you will grant me just a moment to check which of the remaining documents -- Your Honour, if you would allow me just very briefly deal with two documents, I think I can do it in about six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the final aspect I would like to touch upon relates to your time in Prozor, or I'd like to refer you to Exhibit 09994. 09994. This is an ECMM CC Travnik report, a daily summary for the 1st of September, 1993. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, all that I would like to refer you to is on page 2 under the point, Humanitarian, point 4, the first paragraph relates to a meeting with Colonel Siljeg, and there is a confirmed report that 2.000 Muslims from Prozor had been moved to Jablanica, Konjic area. "Siljeg stated this had been done on a voluntary basis." Could you comment on -- on this fact of Muslims moving from Prozor and the numbers perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do go on in the next paragraph to comment by saying, "It seems very unlikely that the Muslims all suddenly decided the time was right to move from Prozor, and coercion is assessed as having played a part; however, the question remains of whether the Muslim authorities in Jablanica were cooperating and ready to receive them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, on this same topic if we can just look at finally Exhibit 09996. 09996.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is CC Mostar daily report for the 10th of September, 1993, and I'd like to refer you to point 5, Humanitarian, and in this paragraph there's a meeting with Ms. Mara Jurkovic social affairs officer in Capljina and it's concerning refugees in the area, "about 6.000 refugees from Kiseljak and may be from Vares," et cetera. Do you have any comments on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It I'm sorry, Mr. Kruger. Are you sure you have 9 September? That's what's in the record and what you said but on my document it says November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies. It is November, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you provide any comment on the mention of 6.000 refugees from Kiseljak who may be from Vares?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry for the hesitation; I was going to make the same point. Yes. "Movement of large-scale numbers through Serb-held territory." Again of interest to us because it was indication of cooperation, and on a scale here would obviously have humanitarian impact as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kruger who would like to begin for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I would be the first one to go. I would note that I'm going to need approximately two minutes or three minutes to set up here, only because I was going through -- keeping track of the documents that we went through, so we could take an early break, and we would have an hour and 40 minutes, or I could just take the two or three minutes to set up. However you wish. I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, we could have the break now and then we would continue nonstop. It is now quarter to 12.00. We will resume at five past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Watkins. I'm Michael Karnavas, with me is Ms. Suzana Tomanovic and together we represent Dr. Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I hope that I didn't alarm you with all my interventions thus far. Sometimes I object for the group, so don't read too much into that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not easily alarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am sure. We're going to start with the general and then we're going to the specific. So, first of all, a little bit about your background. We do know you have an undergraduate degree and master's degree in economics, I think, and political affairs, spent eight years in the military, and spent a considerable amount of time in country; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about what you are not. It might help us a little bit. You're not a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it when you were in country and I mean by that in -- or in theatre, as they would say, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you did not have access to all the legislation, did you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have access to any legislation translated in your language so you could look at, read, analyse, perhaps even consult with one of the other ECMM monitors who, by your own admission, had a legal background?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other monitors that had a legal background, and one tended when we were dealing with legal issues just to sort of point them in that direction. I don't remember having -- we certainly did not have a large-scale body of evidence translated, but there may well have been some documents that were translated for us to give us a steer, but not in-depth, constitutional stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, by the time that you got to the Mostar area, that would have been in October, middle of October, I believe, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was 17th, 18th of October. Yes, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time -- and we need to slow down. I need to slow down. You're doing okay. But at that time, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna had not come into existence; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. I believe it had been formed and announced in August of 1993. But what is true, and we've had reference to earlier, on is the structures were fluid and forming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Suffice it to say that when you got there, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna either was dying off or being transformed into the Croatian republic or had already, when you got there, that you had the Croatian republic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna was formed and in the ascendance and there was no reference during my period except historically to the Croatian Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before going to Mostar or even before going to Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you have access to any literature, and I'm speaking, in particular, Official Gazettes that would have the legislation that established the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have any legal analyses available that someone would have, in other words, taken the legislation, taken the Official Gazettes and had perhaps analysed them, maybe even done a schematic to enable you as a newcomer to have an understanding of at least the political structure?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had an introductory brief on arrival in Zagreb where we were introduced to, and I mean in big broad terms here, the various elements in former Yugoslavia, the issues surrounding communities that were living in the immediate country surrounding, and part of that, my particular interest because I was being sent to Bosnia, was to understand the Bosnian position, but I have to say it was from a low threshold, but I would have been introduced and was introduced to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In a very broad sense?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a very broad political sense, and I do not know whether those that informed me had got their knowledge through direct extraction from legal documents. I think it's unlikely. It's more of a political than a legal analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And also you don't know whether the information that you had received - no disrespect to your colleagues - was accurate?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were always testing information and received wisdoms, but no, there could well have been errors. I'm sure there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And going back to my earlier question, a schematic was not presented to you so you would have the breakup -- breakdown of where the powers lay, the different departments, who had what?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about at the state level concerning what was happening in Sarajevo? Did you ever get a breakdown of how the Sarajevo government was structured?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- no, not ministry by ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you have access to or did you get a briefing on the various peace negotiations that had taken place prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was always of some concern that we on the ground were passing a lot of information up, which we believe was useful to the negotiations, but often were unaware of the detail and how things were forming at a high level. So passages of communication tended to be more up than down the chain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I guess my -- and here's what I'm going to focus on a little bit: By the time you get there, get to Bosnia that is, events -- certain events have already unfolded; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, before the breakout of the war or the break-up of Yugoslavia you have things unfolding; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna being formed after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But I'm going --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm going even before that. On the break-up of Yugoslavia. You're shaking your head. We have to make sure we have a record. So on that, as Yugoslavia is breaking up and as you have various peace negotiations and talks, did you get a briefing book or some sort of briefing that you would at least be able, hitting the ground, to understand what had transpired prior to your arrival and prior to the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a manual, just in broad terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And had you received any briefing, any specific briefing, any -- well, let me just -- let me alter the question slightly. Had you received any concrete and detailed briefing as to what had led -- what were the causes leading up to the situation in Bosnia as it existed at the time that you arrived?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could have a debate about a -- detailed. I was certainly aware of some of the larger dynamics, issues such as the establishment of the Croatian state or the Bosnian state and what had led to those. So in broad terms it, yes, but detailed knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How the function -- how the Sarajevo government functioned, for instance. Did you get a briefing to -- or what existed as far as political structure, you know, and how it operated, and who was -- I mean, we all know Izetbegovic. We've heard of him. Some refer to him always the president, where in fact he was the president of the Presidency, but other than that did you get any detailed briefing on how the Sarajevo government was laid out so at least you could have something concrete to look at perhaps when you're out in the field gathering mention to see whether the information you received is accurate?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the form you're describing. I mean, we were aware of, for instance, municipality elections across the whole of Bosnia. I was aware that he was president of the Presidency but, no, I did not have a schematic diagram and I wouldn't be testing my experiences against that particular diagram. I would be testing my experiences against what I had been told before and then what monitors told me. It was very much heuristic learning, learning as you go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Right. And as I understand someplace you said it took you nearly six months to figure out what was happening?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not six months. I believe, and it was certainly my policy in positions of leadership to just ask monitors to watch and observe and actually shut up for a first few weeks. They needed to absorb, and I actually think it took probably two months before you could begin to understand the complexity, and I think by three or four months you had a real contribution to make. By six months you had achieved a lot. When I say achieved a lot, you would have learned a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You would have a perspective on strategic aims, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going by what you indicated at one point.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated that one of the things that you did when you got to the Mostar area was, you went -- you met with various people in high positions, and it seems to me from reading -- and I've just about read everything that you've said or you made reference to or you wrote. It's obvious to me that you were seeking information at all times; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you're trying to figure out what exactly is happening.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was, and -- yes, that's true, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah. And it's -- often is the case you would go to more than one source, and I believe you used the word "triangulate," in order to figure out what you had heard had any real substance; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Verification of information. Not relying on one source but looking for multiple sources, and then some analysis to make sense of what was emerging.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, while you were doing that, and we're going to get to -- we're going to talk more specifically about that, but I take it while you were in Mostar and even prior to going to Mostar you didn't do the same thing as far as what was happening in Sarajevo or the Muslim government.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what tended to happen is, we -- we had this broad introduction and then as a team member you actually really become involved and quite parochial around your area of responsibility. As you became head of CC, so your geographical and political horizons expanded a little, and by the time I became the head of the regional centre, I was looking at a pan-BiH with also more understanding of what was happening outside of BH. So, yeah, at various times, at various levels, specific references. Where I would point to one thing where we were encouraged in the early days was to think more globally was when we were trying to implement the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, which was -- yes, it had a very local and specific relevance but was seated in a framework of international negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to get to that as well. But this pan-BiH outlook, that might require you to also keep track of what is happening on the international stage as far as negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As best we could, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when we say -- when you use the word "we," is that the imperial we or the we as in the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The imperial. Well, I'm referring really to us as an organisation, but clearly we were a component with a very European perspective, and the UN brought a wider perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I would have been looking at and reading reports not just from ECMM, indeed not just from ECMM in Bosnia. For instance, as the head of the regional centre it I would have been receiving reports from Bulgaria and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But let me stop you here. As far as what was happening -- you mentioned the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Did you have any concrete briefings on that, what was happening in Geneva or what the parties were doing or who was doing what, who was signing what, what the positions were?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, broad. For instance, the ambassador -- sorry, not ambassador. Well, he called him ambassador, actually, Jean-Pierre Thebault who was the head of the regional centre briefed us as head of CC, and I passed down the chain what was going on, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he's briefing you, but did you have any access to documents so that you would have concretely -- you would be aware of what is being proposed, what is being talked about, what are the two sides, the three sides, what their positions are, their respective positions. Did you have that? I'm not talking about the verbal that you're getting.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have very specifically documents stating what had been agreed. So once there was the partial agreement, we did receive documents saying, here are the province boundaries. Here's what to be set up here's how to do it here's who's governing, but with regards to the political discussions that led to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in broad terms in that we got indications of which parties saw a -- which parties were signing and which weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right okay?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when we're talking about, and I'm going to get ahead of myself a little bit, this concept of confederation that has come up, do you know who context that was being discussed at the international level?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in late 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Late 1993. I'm getting ahead of myself --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- because there's a point to that.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have details of what was going on. We were being asked to do things if you remember me saying specifically about what would the -- how would the idea be received of -- of an EU administration in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had these issues about access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly, now let me stop you right there. Access to the sea. That was something that the Bosniaks, the Muslims, wanted; correct? It's a yes or no. We can move along quicker that way. They wanted access to the sea; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the international community thought that if there was to be a settlement, then they would need access to the sea, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on. Hold on. I'm going to stop you here because, you see, you were very accurate when you were answering questions for the Prosecution. I'm not asking what the international community wanted or didn't want. I could care less about them at this point. My question is what the Muslims wanted.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So when we're talking about confederation and I'm asking you, did the Muslims want access to the sea, irrelevant respective of the international thought it might be useful for them to have a deep water port or some place where they could go swimming in the summertime?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to give you a full answer, the Muslims did not want access to the sea because at that time they did not want the break-up of the internationally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that was often the stated case, why should we look at access to the sea? However, if the international community was looking as a particular way forward then access to the sea became an issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was something that was -- so access to the see was something that the internationals were more interested in than the Muslims. I just want to get a -- make sure I understand you.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims -- if there was to be any settlement based on a confederation it would require the Muslims to have access to the sea, but their initial positions were they didn't want to see the break-up. Why should they see the break-up of a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- internationally recognised country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if that was to be the case they would need access and so it was a big issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, since we -- we got ahead of ourselves a little bit, there is one document maybe we should share with the Judges. 7290. It's a Prosecutor's binder. If we could the Prosecutor's binder back with the gentleman. You have it there. And in fact this document might have even been shown to you. Yeah. So we can get this point out of the way real quickly. Incidentally, this confederation, while you are looking for the document, do you know whether any special agreements were reached between BiH and -- and Croatia? Or the Federation, I should say, and Croatia, with respect to confederation?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Part of the Washington Agreement, which formed the federation between the Croats and Muslims, was also insisting on a confederation with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And do we see that also in the -- in the Dayton Accords as well? If you look at --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If we have time we'll get to that as well. If you look at -- on the first page where it says Political, second paragraph, you say -- it says here -- and by the way, did you generate this document? We don't have the -- or you would know from reading -- reading the text.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this is one of my documents, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. It says: "M9 and M2 met Safet? Armija staff officer, 4th Corps, who stated that Muslims were not ready for peace until they had access to the sea. He hoped this would be achieved by political means but ventured that armija would take it by force if necessary. Comment. It is assessed armija do not have the capability for offensive action in the area beyond raids. Comment ends." And the date of this is 21 December 1993. You wrote that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it appear -- at least this particular gentleman seemed to indicate that there was -- there was a -- at some level an indication that they wanted access to the sea and, if necessary, to take it by force.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, going back to where we -- where we were a little bit -- we're still on the background area, when you got to the Croatian -- when you got to the Mostar area, you had already been in country for several months and that was in Central Bosnian; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely. When I began I was in Tomislavgrad, and dealing with Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Jablanica and Bugojno, and I reported to the CC that was based in Grude and then moved to Siroki Brijeg. So my introduction, in fact, to Bosnia was in Herzegovina but very quickly, as I said earlier, began to concentrate in Vrbas valley and then I gravitated north up to the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And you testified in two previous cases. The Kordic case, that was the first case; short?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during your testimony in that case that the Defence in Blaskic had heard that you had not only been testifying but also had given a statement, and then you were called to testify in the Blaskic case as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In Blaskic you testified for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it would appear, if we were to read your testimony, that you were of the opinion, that at least with the relationship between Blaskic and Kordic, Kordic being the -- the civilian, the head of the civilian structure there, had the upper hand in a sense, that he -- he controlled or he could over -- would overrule sometimes Blaskic. I'm simplifying it, but in essence that's what you were testifying to; right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in essence I was, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you've indicated to us today that the situation there was different than the situation you found in Herzegovina. Right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You had plenty it of opportunities to meet with Kordic, by the way?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him on a number of occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You never heard Kordic by the way say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly observe pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it you heard that comment.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it. I'm just trying to find a way of reminding myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we need to look at the monitor. I'm a recidivist and incorrigible but we'll try. All right. You never heard Kordic, for instance, say I got to get instructions or I'm getting instructions or I have been instructed by Prlic in Mostar to do X, Y, and Z?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never had that specific conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it's not matter of having that conversation. When you would approach Kordic, he never gave you an inkling that Jadranko Prlic was above him, directed him, ordered him, and as a consequence he had to comply with whatever, he being Kordic, whatever he was being directed to by Prlic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. My impression was always that his connection was through to Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, one other thing since we're in that area. From your testimony it becomes obvious that at some point the Croatian communities -- there are four pockets, as I understand you put it. Four isolated Croatian pockets?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just rapidly going through my mind as to whether there's four. There were isolated Croat pockets of various sizes, but there were four substantial ones, Vitez, Vares, Zepce, and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just for the record, this could be found in the -- in the Kordic case where the gentleman testified in open session on pages 13099, but it actually starts as early as, I believe, 13096. And you indicated in fact that they were squeezed into four pockets, Vitez, Busovaca, Zepce, Kiseljak, and Vares. You're shaking your head. Does that mean yes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it appeared that the Croats there were not only isolated but there was -- they had some hardships; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there was an issue that came up at some point, and again I'm getting ahead of myself a little bit, about Croats having to leave this it area and going into the Serb area in order to make it down; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were movements of population from Central Bosnia down into Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you say "movements of populations," these folks, these Croats that were living in these pockets were isolated; right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- they were isolated, but they were also different in character. For instance, the pocket in Vares had a common border with Bosnian Serb territory. The pocket around Vitez did not. So they were isolated but with different characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And since they had that common border with the Serbs they could go out that way as opposed to trying to make it, you know, through Muslim-held territory.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now getting back to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Did you actually see any legislation, any decisions, any conclusions, you mentioned a constitution, did you see anything that could be considered legislative instruments that would give you an understanding, at least on paper, at least on paper, how the Croatian republic was formed or being formed?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian republic or the Croatian Community?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Croatian republic. I'm not asking for what you had heard. I'm asking whether you had seen, like Official Gazettes or documents that were translated to you so that you could look at, study them, and then say, okay, now I understand the structure.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but what was interesting in my inquiries was that the structure was obviously very fluid, and I'm not sure whether that detail was that you're suggesting was there in existence. If it was, then it was only known by a few because what was clear is there were many contradictions in who was filling certain roles and posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you speak of contradictions, and I would agree with you that at least from listening to your testimony that you were getting mixed messages at times, but those were oral messages from personalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you had a language assistant?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Several of them. And -- and I take it they were from the area?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Mostar they were from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you ever ask your language assistants to try to get a hold of for you any documents that were being generated showing the establishment and the functioning of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? It's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just pausing for the interpreters. I'm remembering this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do that. Do that. Pause.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one clarification, actually. I remember that one of the interpreters actually came from Croatia itself, but from Split. Now, to specifically answer your question, I would dearly have loved to have got those documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is the answer no?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we tried to get those documents but I'm not sure they were in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the answer is, I did not have any Gazettes or legislative papers to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay now, you say they were not in existence. Now, again, let's fast forward a little bit with Jadranko Prlic. I've sat here and I've listened to you, and I've also read some of the documents that were generated, and you've indicated quite readily that you had a good working relationship with him.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That he -- you said, "easy accession and open discussions." That was a quote, I think.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, he was the type of individual that readily accessible, especially to meet with internationals.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you knew that -- you're shaking your head. That means yes?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact that's why when there would be some VIPs, you knew at least Jadranko Prlic would be one of the -- the officials in Mostar that they could have access to; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that it was worth them seeing him because of his position in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And, of course, when you asked him questions he answered them?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, usually straightforwardly. Not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't see in the documents and maybe there are some in the ECMM archive, wherever that might be I'd like to spend some time but I only have what limited documents the Prosecution has given us, but I don't see anywhere you concretely having asked Jadranko Prlic a specific question and then in your comment you say he was evasive, he refused to answer, he gave you bogus information. There's nothing there that at least I have been able to it find in the documents that the ECMM provided to the Prosecution for your testimony and for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should be spared having to read all the ECMM reports, but I do believe that in there, there will be times when we asked questions, and indeed I remember one when we were asking Mr. Prlic about movement of -- exchange of prisoners and movement of humanitarian aid when he was evasive, but diplomatically pointing me to Mr. Pusic who should answer those questions. So we didn't always get the information we want but we were dealing with someone who was willing to discuss more broadly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's why I asked you. That's why I asked you earlier if you had seen the schematic and if you had seen any legislation to actually have an understanding as to who had what authority, and who had what responsibility, and who was able to do what with whom and under what circumstances; that's why I asked you that question. And the answer was, I believe, you hadn't looked at and -- or you said that you didn't have access to any of those documents.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I did not have access to those documents. What I was doing was actually trying to create that structure through the analysis and the questions I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, had you had access to the documents and I'm not suggesting that you did not, but had you -- if you had those documents, if you knew -- especially for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna you would have been able -- those were available, but also we'll suggest and show that others were available. Do you think you might have been able to -- from those documents with your education and background, if they had been properly translated, would they have been able to assist you in knowing who had what power and what responsibility and what authority?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Clearly they would have helped. I do remember that we did get some information about the structure of the HDZ and who was going to hold particular positions, with Pero Markovic identified as the senior. So we'd got -- and that was in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't mean to cut you off because I'm really under a tremendous amount of stress with the time, but HDZ is a party; right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're talking about a political process. All right? So if I ask you, for instance, how does the political process in the UK functions, you're not going to talk to me about the labour party or the conservatives. You're going to describe to me, you know, how it functions, right? How the parliament works and so on and so forth; correct?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if it was a single party state it would be pointless to describe that constitution to you without also taking reference to the other -- the fact that there was only one party, and I believe I gave a statement yesterday where part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, certainly information that I got was that HDZ was to be the party and that other small ones --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- were not recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: So HDZ was very important to understand in the structure of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was -- now, does that mean that also Jadranko Prlic was a member of the HDZ. It's a yes, it's a no, it's a maybe, it's an I don't know. Those are the four choices and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a pause for the interpreters and then I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I -- okay. You can't remember. But if we were to take your previous answer, one would automatically conclude that if you had to be a player and there was only one player, then you had to be a member of this party; correct? So at least based on your assumptions, and I underscore the word "assumptions," that's what you're -- that's what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd go along with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, also from listening to you, it was my understanding, and correct me if I'm wrong, that it was your understanding that the process was somewhat flawed because you would have expected members of parliament or members of the government to come from the members of the parliament. Do I have that wrong or is that what you --

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did think the process was deeply flawed but for a number of reasons and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was one of them?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've picked out one there, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it in the UK, and I follow politics a little bit in the UK, fascinating, one does have to be elected in order to be a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not strictly true. You can be a member the of the government and sit in the House of Lords, the second Chamber, and -- but the House of Lords is not an elected body. One of the lovely quirks of the British constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that allows you to have a seat on the government?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it can. I can give you a high profile example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't need one. I just want to -- I'm just using this as an example. Would it surprise you, sir, if I were to tell you that under the process that existed there in -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and if I'm not mistaken, it still exists, that you cannot be a member of the parliament and at the same time -- which is a legislative body, and at the same time be a member of the executive it? Would it surprise you to learn that you can't be in both? You have to be either in one or the other.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you -- did you -- did you ask Jadranko Prlic to explain to you exactly how the Croatian republic was structured from a political sense?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it he sat down -- did he ever do a schematic for you so you could understand it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember doing any schematics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He did, however, invite you when they had that opening congress, if we want to call it that?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very generous and helped me with my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's the Assembly session. We have to be correct. My colleague here is reprimanding me. All right. And it was a rather transparent process?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was surprisingly so to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Especially you standing there. You had your white uniform sticking out. And so Mr. Jadranko Prlic at the time had nothing to hide and -- right?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he might have wanted me to see things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he wanted you to learn some things as well.

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- so there was nothing -- nothing secretive about what was happening, what was said, and everything that was happening and being said was available for you not only to see and hear but to pass on?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ask him to sit on any other sessions?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Suffice it to say any time you wanted to see him he was available for you?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, good access to Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, very quickly if we could go through some documents. And I guess I want to -- at first I want to start with a couple of housekeeping matters. If we could go to document 6303, and it's in the Prosecutor's binder. You might recall the passage that was shown to you earlier, and I want to clarify a couple of points because this document will indeed be introduced by the Prosecution, and on the very first page we see that it's October 31, 1993. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the paper. This is a report which I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the political section and if you go to the second paragraph, and it says here -- I mean, you're being -- earlier you talked about Stupni Do a little bit, but then it says, "Prlic stated that Bosnia-Herzegovina would never exit as a state but all other options were possible." Now, my question is: Do you allow for the possibility, sir, that perhaps you're missing one particular word, and that word may be "unitary"? Would never exist as a unitary state?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the way I would interpret what he said to me, as that it would not remain as a unitary state with its authority all vested in Sarajevo but would be some other configuration, and most likely a three-republic configuration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But he never called for the eradication [Realtime transcript read in error "ratification"] of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state?

utterances.speaker: PHILIP ROGER WATKINS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but one could conclude that by setting up a self-styled republic within the existing state you could be sending some pretty strong signals about the break-up of Bosnia, but certainly he was talking at that time about within the existing international borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, didn't that call for something like republics in a state? Now, surely you're not suggesting that Lord Owen and Stoltenberg had -- were planning on breaking up Bosnia-Herzegovina because they were suggesting that one way to resolve this issue where you have three constituent peoples would be to have three republics within a state?
